findings.title: Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags contain six r.log.Error calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) that log normal, successful operation: "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Tags to clean", "cleaned tags". These fire on every batch of every cleanup run even when nothing is wrong (the "err" kv is always nil at those points), and they log the complete slice of IDs to be deleted, which can be up to the configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries in a single line. Combined with the cleanup ticker being changed to 1 minute in this PR, this floods error-level logs during healthy operation, breaks any alerting based on error logs, and can produce enormous log lines for large batch sizes. These are leftover debug statements and should be r.log.Debug at most, and probably should not dump the raw ID list.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, running all cleanup jobs 10x more often
findings.body: The Run loop ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. clean() does not only run annotation cleanup — on every tick it runs the entire job list: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, expiring user invites, deleting stale short URLs, two query-history enforcement queries, and re-scanning the temp file directories. This change therefore multiplies the database and filesystem load of all background cleanup jobs by 10, yet the PR description (about avoiding MySQL deadlocks in annotation cleanup) never mentions it. If the intent is to keep annotation cleanup batches small and frequent, that should be scoped to the annotation job or at least called out explicitly; as written this is an undocumented behavior change affecting every cleanup task.

findings.title: SQLite literal IN-list built with O(n^2) string concatenation
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback for batch sizes over 999 builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over ids. Each iteration allocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building the list is quadratic in the number of IDs. With the batch size exercised in the new test (32767 IDs) this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch, and it runs on every batch iteration of the cleanup loop. Use a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-converted strings) to make it linear.

findings.title: Parameter-limit guard only covers SQLite; large batch sizes break on Postgres
findings.body: deleteByIDs only sidesteps bind-parameter limits when the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999; every other database gets a `DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` statement with one placeholder per ID. Postgres rejects statements with more than 65535 bind parameters, and very large placeholder lists can also hit MySQL's max_allowed_packet. Since AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable and the PR itself tests a value of 32767, a batch size above 65535 on Postgres would make the delete fail on every cleanup cycle (the job errors out and nothing is cleaned). Consider chunking the ID list into fixed-size DELETE batches for all dialects instead of special-casing SQLite.
